Lola Nena's kitchen
Hey, good question, Lola! Let us find out how these guesses work.
Come on, let us look inside the guess!
AI learns patterns from many examples, then makes a guess.

Show a computer thousands of mango photos and it learns what mangoes usually look like. Then it can guess if a new photo shows a mango. It is a guess from patterns, not magic and not a mind. Your phone is not listening: it is guessing what you might like.
Three parts of every AI guess
Tap each part to see what it means.
Examples
Lots of photos, words or numbers the AI is shown first.
Patterns
What the examples have in common, like shapes and colours.
Guess
An answer for something new. It can be right or wrong.
Examples, patterns, guess. You have got this!
A computer saw 1,000 mango photos. What did it learn?
What mangoes taste like
Not quite. It only saw pictures, so it cannot know a taste.
Patterns of shape and colour
Yes! It learned what mangoes usually look like, nothing more.
How to grow a mango tree
No. Photos show how a mango looks, not how it grows.
AI you already use
Tap each one to see the guess it makes for you.
Guesses which posts you will watch, like or share, and shows those first.
Guesses where your eyes, nose and mouth are, so the puppy ears stay put.
Maps traffic
Guesses your travel time from patterns in past traffic.
Guesses which messages are junk because it has seen many junk messages before.
Guesses the words you said from the sound of your voice.
Symptom checker
Guesses what might be going on from patterns in past cases. It cannot examine you.
See? AI is hiding in plain sight. Each one is a guess.
Your maps app says "20 minutes". Is that a promise or a guess?
A promise: the app knows the future
No. Nobody knows the future, not even a smart app. A flood or an accident can change it.
A guess from patterns in past traffic
Yes! It is usually a good guess, so use it, but leave a little extra time.
AI in health: it helps, people decide
Tap each one to see how AI is used, and who still decides.
X-ray helpers
Mark spots on a scan so a doctor looks closely. The doctor makes the call.
Health chatbots
Answer simple questions and point you to a clinic. They can be wrong, so do not use them to diagnose.
Appointment systems
Guess busy hours to shorten the queue. Staff still run the clinic.
Claims-fraud flags
Flag odd insurance claims for a person to check. A flag is not a verdict.
AI helps; people decide. Remember that!
A tea box says "AI-powered formula". Does that sticker make it work?
Yes, AI proves it works
No. "AI-powered" is a sticker, not proof. Anyone can print it on a box.
No. Check if it is registered with the FDA
Yes! Check the FDA, and ask a health worker before you trust a health claim.
Stickers are cheap. Proof is not.
Where did you meet AI this week?
In my social media feed
In a camera filter
In a maps or ride app
I am not sure
Thank you! There is no wrong answer. AI is often hiding in ordinary apps, so being not sure is normal.
Trust AI for low-stakes guesses, like traffic or spam, and double-check the ones that matter.
"AI-powered" is a sticker, not proof.
For health decisions, a health worker decides.
Bea's school project
Let's teach a computer to catch fake health posts!
Ooh, a school project! Let us find out what a computer can learn.
Come on, let us teach it and see what happens!
AI only knows what it was shown.

An AI learns from the examples people give it, and nothing else. If it never saw a ripe mango, it has no idea what one is. It only knows what it was taught. Good examples make a good helper. Missing examples make blind spots.
A fruit sorter was trained only on green mangoes. Then it sees a ripe yellow mango. What does it say?
"Mango!" It knows every kind
No. It only knows what it was shown, and it never saw a yellow one.
"Not a mango"
Yes! Green was all it learned, so yellow looks like something new. Missing examples make blind spots.
"I am not sure, please ask a person"
That would be wise, but most AI is not built to say it. It usually just answers.
Lopsided examples, unfair results
Tap each one to see how lopsided examples hurt real people.
Trained mostly on one accent, it keeps misunderstanding Bisaya speakers. The people were fine. The examples were lopsided.
Photo app
Trained mostly on lighter faces, it makes more mistakes on darker faces. Whoever is missing from the examples pays for it.
Health app
Trained on city clinic records, it can miss what is common in the province. Check that it was trained on people like you.
Lopsided examples make lopsided AI. We call that bias.
An AI says "98% sure". Does a high number mean it is right?
Yes, 98% sure means it is right
Not always. The number shows how sure the AI feels, not whether it is correct.
No. It can be confidently wrong
Yes! AI can say a wrong answer in a very sure voice. A big number is not proof, so check anything important.
Sure is not the same as right. You will see that in the game!
"Why did the AI say that?"
Tap each tile to see what a fair "why?" gives you.
Highlighted words
A detector can show the words it leaned on. If they are silly words, you know not to trust the answer.
Words it never saw
It cannot use words it was never taught. A post in your language may look like a blank to it.
A fair question
You can always ask an AI tool, or the people who made it, "Why did it say that?" A good tool can show you.
Asking "why?" is not rude. It is how you stay in charge.
Balanced or lopsided?
Lopsided
A skin-check app trained on photos of only one skin tone
Lopsided: it will guess worse on the skin tones it never saw.
A voice assistant trained on many accents from across the Philippines
Balanced: many kinds of speakers means fewer people left out.
A fake-post detector trained only on English posts
Lopsided: it has seen no Taglish or Bisaya posts.
A flu-risk tool trained on records from towns and cities, young and old
Balanced: it learned from different places and ages.
A fruit sorter that saw only green mangoes
Lopsided: ripe mangoes are a blind spot.
A spam filter trained on both junk and normal messages in Tagalog, Bisaya and English
Balanced: both kinds of messages, in the languages people use.
Would you trust a detector trained only in English to check posts in your language?
Yes, I would trust it
Only a little
